title: Markdown Blog with Next.js
tagline: Build a fully-featured developer blog using Next.js App Router, file-system MDX, Tailwind CSS, and syntax-highlighted code blocks — zero CMS required.

phases.title: Project Setup & Folder Structure
phases.content:
# Phase 1 — Project Setup & Folder Structure

## 🎯 What You Will Accomplish

Boot a clean Next.js 14 project with TypeScript and Tailwind, install every dependency you need for the rest of the project, and establish the folder architecture that all future phases build on.

By the end of this phase you will have a working dev server and a clear file structure to follow.

---

## 💡 Core Concepts

### Why Next.js App Router?
The App Router (introduced in Next.js 13, the default since 14) lets every component be a **React Server Component** by default.

This means your blog's reading pages:
- Are **rendered entirely on the server** — zero JavaScript sent to the browser for the reading experience
- Have **instant time-to-first-byte** — served as pre-rendered HTML
- Can **read files directly** using Node.js `fs` — no API call needed

### File-System Routing
In the App Router, every `page.tsx` inside `app/` becomes a URL automatically.

| File | URL |
|---|---|
| `app/page.tsx` | `/` |
| `app/blog/page.tsx` | `/blog` |
| `app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx` | `/blog/your-post-slug` |

No explicit route config. No framework magic to learn. Just files.

### Why gray-matter?
`gray-matter` parses the **frontmatter block** at the top of Markdown files — the YAML section between `---` delimiters. It splits any `.md` file into:
- `data` — the metadata (title, date, tags)
- `content` — the actual Markdown prose

This lets you store structured metadata alongside your writing without a database.

---

## 🛠 Step-by-Step Instructions

### Step 1 · Create the Next.js project

Open your terminal and run these commands:

```bash
npx create-next-app@latest my-blog \
  --typescript \
  --tailwind \
  --eslint \
  --app \
  --src-dir=false \
  --import-alias "@/*"

cd my-blog
```

> **What each flag does**
> - `--typescript` — TypeScript from day one, catches type errors before they become runtime bugs
> - `--tailwind` — Wires up Tailwind's PostCSS plugin automatically
> - `--app` — Uses the new App Router directory (`app/`)
> - `--src-dir=false` — Keeps `app/` at the root, not inside a `src/` folder
> - `--import-alias "@/*"` — Allows `@/lib/posts` instead of `../../lib/posts`

### Step 2 · Install project dependencies

```bash
npm install gray-matter react-markdown remark-gfm rehype-highlight
```

| Package | What it does |
|---|---|
| `gray-matter` | Parses YAML frontmatter from `.md` files |
| `react-markdown` | Renders Markdown as React components |
| `remark-gfm` | Adds GitHub Flavored Markdown (tables, task lists, strikethrough) |
| `rehype-highlight` | Syntax-highlights fenced code blocks via highlight.js |

### Step 3 · Create the folder structure

From the project root:

```bash
mkdir -p content/posts
mkdir -p lib
mkdir -p components
```

Your full directory tree should look like this:

```
my-blog/
├── app/
│   ├── layout.tsx          ← root layout: html, body, global nav
│   ├── page.tsx            ← homepage: list of all posts
│   ├── globals.css
│   └── blog/
│       └── [slug]/
│           └── page.tsx    ← individual post page
├── content/
│   └── posts/
│       ├── hello-world.md
│       └── understanding-closures.md
├── lib/
│   └── posts.ts            ← file-system helpers (read, list, parse)
├── components/
│   ├── PostCard.tsx        ← card shown on the homepage
│   └── Prose.tsx           ← styled markdown renderer
├── next.config.ts
├── package.json
└── tsconfig.json
```

### Step 4 · Verify the dev server starts

```bash
npm run dev
```

Open `http://localhost:3000`. You should see the default Next.js splash page.

If it loads — you're ready to build.

---

## ✅ Phase Checkpoint

Before marking this phase complete, verify all of these:

- [ ] `npm run dev` starts without errors in the terminal
- [ ] `http://localhost:3000` loads in the browser
- [ ] The `content/posts/` directory exists at the project root
- [ ] Running `npm list gray-matter` shows a version number
- [ ] `tsconfig.json` has `"@/*": ["./*"]` in the `paths` section

---

> **🧠 Key takeaway:** Next.js App Router uses file-system routing — every `page.tsx` is a URL. Server Components can read from the filesystem directly. This is the foundation everything else in this project builds on.

# Phase 5 — Deployment to Vercel

## 🎯 What You Will Accomplish

Deploy your blog to Vercel's global edge network with a real `.vercel.app` domain. Set up automatic deployments so every `git push` to `main` publishes a new version. Optionally add a custom domain.

---

## 💡 Core Concepts

### Why Vercel?
Vercel built Next.js. Their platform:
- **Auto-detects** Next.js and configures the build correctly — no config file needed
- **Preview deployments** — every pull request gets its own live URL automatically
- **Static pages served from CDN** — your blog posts load in < 100ms globally

### Static vs Dynamic in production
Because you used `generateStaticParams`, every post is a **static HTML file** at build time:
```
✅  /                    → static
✅  /blog/hello-world    → static
✅  /blog/understanding-closures → static
```
Zero server-side rendering. Zero cold starts. Just CDN-served HTML.

### Build verification
Always run `npm run build` locally before pushing. It catches:
- TypeScript type errors
- Missing imports
- Pages that fail to statically generate

---

## 🛠 Step-by-Step Instructions

### Step 1 · Verify the production build locally

```bash
npm run build
```

Look for output like this — all pages should be ○ (static):

```
Route (app)                     Size
┌ ○ /                          1.2 kB
├ ○ /blog/hello-world          892 B
└ ○ /blog/understanding-closures  912 B

○  (Static) prerendered as static content
```

If there are errors — fix them before continuing.

### Step 2 · Push to GitHub

```bash
# Initialize git (if you haven't already)
git init
git add .
git commit -m "feat: complete markdown blog"

# Create a repo on github.com, then:
git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/my-blog.git
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main
```

> **Security check:** Make sure `.gitignore` includes `.env.local` and `node_modules`.

### Step 3 · Import to Vercel

1. Go to [vercel.com](https://vercel.com) and sign in with GitHub
2. Click **Add New → Project**
3. Find your `my-blog` repository → click **Import**
4. Leave all settings at defaults — Vercel auto-detects Next.js
5. Click **Deploy**

First deployment takes ~60 seconds. You'll get a URL like `my-blog-xyz.vercel.app`.

### Step 4 · Verify the live deployment

Open your `.vercel.app` URL and confirm:
- The homepage loads with both posts
- Clicking a post title opens the full post with syntax highlighting
- Check the browser DevTools Network tab — HTML is served instantly (static)

### Step 5 · Add a custom domain (optional)

1. In Vercel project dashboard → **Settings → Domains**
2. Type your domain (e.g. `myblog.dev`) → click **Add**
3. Copy the `CNAME` or `A` record shown
4. Add it in your domain registrar's DNS settings
5. Vercel auto-provisions an SSL certificate via Let's Encrypt

### Step 6 · Set up auto-deployments

This already works! Every time you:

```bash
git add content/posts/new-post.md
git commit -m "post: my new article"
git push origin main
```

Vercel automatically runs a new build and deploys within ~60 seconds.

---

## ✅ Phase Checkpoint

- [ ] `npm run build` completes with zero errors
- [ ] All routes show ○ (static) in the build output
- [ ] Vercel dashboard shows a successful deployment (green checkmark)
- [ ] Your `.vercel.app` URL loads the homepage and individual posts
- [ ] Pushing a new commit to `main` triggers a new deployment

---

## 🏆 Project Complete!

You built and shipped a **production markdown blog**. Here's what you now understand deeply:

- **Next.js App Router** — file-system routing, Server Components, layouts
- **Static generation** — `generateStaticParams`, CDN-first architecture
- **File-system content layer** — gray-matter, `fs.readFileSync`, `process.cwd()`
- **Markdown rendering pipeline** — remark → rehype → React
- **Production deployment** — Vercel, CDN, preview deployments, custom domains

**Your next challenge:**
- Add a tag filter page (`/blog/tag/[tag]`)
- Add an RSS feed (`/feed.xml`)
- Add dark/light theme toggle
- Add full-text search with Fuse.js

> **🧠 Key takeaway:** You built a database-free, server-free, CDN-hosted blog. This architecture scales to millions of readers at near-zero cost. The same pattern powers documentation sites at Stripe, Vercel, and Linear.

phases.title: Architecture & Project Scaffolding
phases.content:
# Phase 1 — Architecture & Project Scaffolding

## 🎯 What You Will Accomplish

Scaffold a production-grade Express + TypeScript project with a **layered MVC architecture**, validated environment configuration, and a working health-check endpoint. This is the foundation everything else builds on.

---

## 💡 Core Concepts

### Layered Architecture

Instead of writing all logic in route handlers ("fat controllers"), we split responsibilities:

```
 HTTP Request
     ↓
  Router        — maps method + path → controller function
     ↓
  Controller    — validates input, calls service, formats response
     ↓
  Service       — business logic (what the app does)
     ↓
  Repository    — database access (how data is stored/retrieved)
     ↓
  Database
```

**Why?** Each layer can be tested independently. You can swap PostgreSQL for SQLite in tests. You can change your business logic without touching route definitions.

### Why Validate Environment Variables?

Don't trust `process.env` to have what you need. If `DATABASE_URL` is missing, you want the server to crash **immediately with a clear error**, not fail silently on the first database query 5 minutes later.

`envalid` validates and coerces env vars at startup:

```typescript
const env = cleanEnv(process.env, {
  DATABASE_URL: str(),   // crashes if missing
  PORT: port({ default: 4000 }),  // number type, has a default
});
```

### Express Middleware Stack

Middleware runs top-to-bottom on every request:

```
Request → helmet() → cors() → json() → router → errorHandler
```

- **helmet** — sets security HTTP headers (prevents clickjacking, XSS, etc.)
- **cors** — controls which origins can call the API
- **json** — parses request bodies as JSON

---

## 🛠 Step-by-Step Instructions

### Step 1 · Initialize the project

```bash
mkdir my-api && cd my-api
npm init -y
```

### Step 2 · Install all dependencies

```bash
# Runtime dependencies
npm install express cors helmet envalid dotenv

# TypeScript + type definitions
npm install -D typescript ts-node-dev @types/express @types/cors @types/node
```

### Step 3 · Configure TypeScript

Create `tsconfig.json`:

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2022",
    "module": "CommonJS",
    "rootDir": "src",
    "outDir": "dist",
    "strict": true,
    "esModuleInterop": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true,
    "resolveJsonModule": true
  },
  "include": ["src/**/*"],
  "exclude": ["node_modules", "dist"]
}
```

### Step 4 · Add npm scripts

Update `package.json`:

```json
"scripts": {
  "dev": "ts-node-dev --respawn --transpile-only src/index.ts",
  "build": "tsc",
  "start": "node dist/index.js"
}
```

### Step 5 · Create the folder structure

```bash
mkdir -p src/{config,controllers,services,repositories,routes,middleware,types}
```

Full directory tree:

```
src/
├── config/
│   ├── env.ts          ← validated environment variables
│   └── prisma.ts       ← Prisma client singleton (Phase 2)
├── controllers/
│   ├── auth.controller.ts
│   └── task.controller.ts
├── services/
│   └── task.service.ts
├── repositories/
│   └── task.repository.ts
├── routes/
│   ├── index.ts        ← master router
│   ├── auth.routes.ts
│   └── task.routes.ts
├── middleware/
│   ├── errorHandler.ts ← global error handler
│   ├── notFound.ts     ← 404 handler
│   └── authenticate.ts ← JWT guard (Phase 3)
├── types/
│   └── express.d.ts    ← augmented Request type
└── index.ts            ← app entry point
```

### Step 6 · Set up environment validation

Create `.env`:

```bash
NODE_ENV=development
PORT=4000
DATABASE_URL=postgresql://postgres:password@localhost:5432/myapi
JWT_SECRET=change-me-to-a-long-random-secret-min-32-chars
CORS_ORIGIN=http://localhost:3000
```

Create `src/config/env.ts`:

```typescript
import { cleanEnv, str, port } from 'envalid';

export const env = cleanEnv(process.env, {
  NODE_ENV: str({
    choices: ['development', 'test', 'production'],
    default: 'development',
  }),
  PORT: port({ default: 4000 }),
  DATABASE_URL: str(),
  JWT_SECRET: str(),
  CORS_ORIGIN: str({ default: 'http://localhost:3000' }),
});
```

### Step 7 · Build the Express app

Create `src/index.ts`:

```typescript
import 'dotenv/config';
import express from 'express';
import cors from 'cors';
import helmet from 'helmet';
import { env } from './config/env';

const app = express();

// Security + parsing middleware
app.use(helmet());
app.use(cors({ origin: env.CORS_ORIGIN, credentials: true }));
app.use(express.json());

// Health check — always the first real route
app.get('/health', (_req, res) => {
  res.json({
    status: 'ok',
    uptime: Math.floor(process.uptime()),
    environment: env.NODE_ENV,
  });
});

// TODO Phase 2: mount routers here
// app.use('/api', router);

app.listen(env.PORT, () => {
  console.log(`🚀 Server running → http://localhost:${env.PORT}`);
  console.log(`   Environment: ${env.NODE_ENV}`);
});

export default app;
```

### Step 8 · Test it

```bash
npm run dev
curl http://localhost:4000/health
```

Expected response:
```json
{ "status": "ok", "uptime": 2, "environment": "development" }
```

---

## ✅ Phase Checkpoint

- [ ] `npm run dev` starts without TypeScript errors
- [ ] `GET http://localhost:4000/health` returns `{ "status": "ok" }`
- [ ] Removing `DATABASE_URL` from `.env` causes the server to crash with a clear message
- [ ] `.env` is listed in `.gitignore`
- [ ] The `src/` folder structure matches the tree above

---

> **🧠 Key takeaway:** The layered architecture is what separates hobby projects from production codebases. When your test suite mocks the Repository layer, your Service layer tests run 100x faster — and your business logic is proven correct before a single database query runs.
